title: Replication Through Removable Media
summary: Replication through removable media moves code onto new systems by writing malicious files to USB flash drives, external disks, memory cards or mobile devices and relying on the media being inserted somewhere else. Attackers either drop an executable with a convincing document-like name or icon and wait for a curious user, or they replace an existing file on the drive so an authorised operator carries the payload across a boundary. Older systems may still honour Autorun or Autoplay entries that execute a program on insertion without any user action, and some incidents abuse the device firmware or the process used to format the media so the code is present before the drive leaves the supplier. Mobile phones and even charging cables have been used as the carrier because a phone can present itself as a mounted storage device. Defenders work from device connection records, file-write telemetry to removable volumes, created Autorun files, and image-load events on unusual paths.

beginner.definition: Replication through removable media means an attacker copies harmful software onto a USB stick, external drive or phone and lets someone carry it to another computer. When the device is plugged in, the software runs and the attacker gains a foothold. It is a way to spread into networks that have little or no internet connection.
beginner.whyItMatters: Some important networks are deliberately kept off the internet, for example in factories, hospitals or power stations. A USB stick is one of the few things that crosses that gap. Attackers know this, so they use removable media when a network cannot be reached online. If you ignore it, a single forgotten drive can undo years of network separation.
howItWorks: The attacker writes malware onto a removable drive, often hiding it among normal files.
The file may be renamed or given an icon that looks like a document or photo.
Autorun is a Windows setting that lets a drive start a program the moment it is inserted.
If Autorun is enabled, the program runs with no click from the user at all.
Otherwise the user opens the fake document and runs the hidden program by mistake.
The malware copies itself to other connected drives so the cycle repeats.
beginner.example: Imagine a hospital night desk where staff carry paper notes between two buildings because the phone lines are cut. Anyone can slip a fake note into that pile, and the night nurse will read it as normal business. The paper is trusted because it arrived by hand, not by post. A USB drive works the same way between a normal office network and an isolated machine.
takeaways: Removable media is one of the few paths that crosses into networks kept off the internet.
Turn off Autorun and Autoplay so inserting a drive cannot run anything by itself.
Log and review every removable device connection on sensitive machines.

objectives: Explain how removable media can carry malware into a network with no internet access.
Describe the roles of Autorun and of disguised file names in this technique.
Identify the telemetry, such as device connection records and file writes to removable volumes, that reveals it.
Distinguish authorised use of USB drives from suspicious writes to those drives.
Summarise the controls, including Autorun disablement and device control policy, that reduce the risk.
